sentences.text: The genus name Tromerosaurus combines the Ancient Greek words tromerós, meaning 'terrible' or 'frightening', and saûros, meaning 'lizard'.

The holotype is an incomplete but articulated skeleton containing most of the skull and the majority of the postcranium, including neck and trunk vertebrae, ribs, gastralia, both upper arms, the pelvis, and most of the right leg.
Digital reconstruction suggests the skull of the holotype reaches a length of up to 90 centimeters.
The femur of the holotype measures 95 centimeters in length.
The snout accounts for more than 60% of the skull length, maintaining a relatively consistent height from the snout to the back of the skull.
The holotype possesses 13 maxillary teeth, contrasting with 15 teeth found in the referred specimen TMP 1994.012.0602.
The dentary of the holotype has 16 teeth, falling within the range of 15 to 18 seen in Gorgosaurus.
Stuart Plotkin discovered the holotype skeleton of Tromerosaurus in 2010 in the upper Oldman Formation in Alberta, Canada.
Stuart Plotkin discovered tyrannosaurid remains in the upper zone of the Oldman Formation near the Provincial Dinosaur Park in Alberta, Canada, in 2010.
A team from the University of Alberta assisted in the excavation of the specimen between 2010 and 2011.
The holotype specimen is cataloged as UALVP 52981 and is housed at the University of Alberta's Vertebrate Paleontology Laboratory.
Mark J. Powers and colleagues described Tromerosaurus solumons as a new tyrannosaurid genus and species in 2026, designating UALVP 52981 as the holotype.
Two isolated maxillae from unknown localities were tentatively referred to the species, representing a mature individual and a small juvenile.
Two isolated maxillae from unknown deposits were tentatively referred to the species: UALVP 56605 from a mature individual and TMP 1985.011.0003 from a small juvenile.
Tromerosaurus lived during the Campanian age of the Late Cretaceous in Canada.
Tromerosaurus is classified within the subfamily Albertosaurinae, though it shares some features with tyrannosaurines.
Parsimony analyses recovered Tromerosaurus as the most basal member of the subfamily Albertosaurinae.

In all most parsimonious versions of their analyses, Powers et al. recovered Tromerosaurus as the most basal member of the subfamily Albertosaurinae, which also includes Albertosaurus and Gorgosaurus.
Bayesian analyses by Powers et al. (2026) placed Tromerosaurus as the most basal member of the subfamily Tyrannosaurinae, conflicting with parsimony results.

In contrast to their parsimony results, the Bayesian analysis by Powers et al. (2026) placed Tromerosaurus as the most basal member of the subfamily Tyrannosaurinae, the sister group to Albertosaurinae.
The conflicting phylogenetic results highlight a mosaic anatomy in Tromerosaurus, featuring traits of both albertosaurines and early tyrannosaurines.
